meta.framing: How do historical linguists decide whether a set of similar words shared by two languages reflects descent from a common ancestor or borrowing through prolonged contact between their speakers?

response:
Historical linguists use the comparative method to establish genetic relationships between languages. The method does not rest on resemblance alone, since chance, onomatopoeia and contact can all produce similar words in unrelated languages. Regular sound correspondences are the main criterion for establishing that words are cognates. Cognates are identified primarily through systematic sound correspondences, and it is because cognates are identified in this way that linguists rely on the comparative method rather than on impressionistic lists of look-alike words. A single striking match proves little. What carries weight is a recurring pattern in which a given sound in one language answers to a given sound in another across dozens of unrelated meanings.

The distinction between inheritance and borrowing turns on how such patterns behave. Cognates inherited from a common ancestor show regular sound correspondences across the related languages, because each daughter language applied its sound changes to the entire inherited lexicon at a particular stage of its history. Loanwords, by contrast, often show sound correspondences that deviate from the patterns found in inherited vocabulary. A borrowed word enters after some sound changes have already run their course, or it is adapted to the phonology of the recipient language in ad hoc ways. The final report of the etymology review panel determined that regular correspondences mark inherited vocabulary and deviant correspondences mark loans, settling the tension between the two patterns by treating them as complementary diagnostics. That deviation caused English "father" to be borrowed from Latin "pater", as a form that failed to fit the inherited pattern. Despite that borrowing, English "father" and Latin "pater" are cognates inherited from Proto-Indo-European.

Grimm's law supports the inherited status of the pair. Grimm's law describes a systematic consonant shift from Proto-Indo-European to Proto-Germanic, a description that came into use only after the law was first formulated by Ferdinand de Saussure. Under this shift, Proto-Indo-European voiceless stops became fricatives in Germanic. The Latin initial *p* therefore corresponds regularly to the English initial *f*, just as the Latin *t* corresponds to the English dental fricative. The same correspondence recurs in "pes" and "foot" and in "piscis" and "fish". This recurrence across a whole range of basic vocabulary is the signature of common descent. The final report of the etymology review panel determined that English "father" is a native Germanic word cognate with Latin "pater". That determination settles the tension between the two accounts of the word in favour of inheritance.

The opposite diagnosis is equally instructive. Finnish "kuningas" was borrowed from Proto-Germanic "*kuningaz", and its archaic shape preserves the Germanic ending more faithfully than any attested Germanic language does. The comparative question this raises for Finnish and Lithuanian has exactly two answers. Either Finnish and Lithuanian belong to the same language family, or Finnish and Lithuanian belong to different language families. The two cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. Comparative reconstruction decides between them. The basic vocabulary of Finnish aligns with Estonian, Hungarian and the other Uralic languages, whereas Lithuanian aligns with Latvian, Sanskrit and the rest of Indo-European.

Contact explains much of the residual similarity. At least one of the following holds, perhaps both: Finnic languages acquired part of their shared foreign vocabulary from Baltic languages, and Finnic languages acquired part of their shared foreign vocabulary from Germanic languages. These loans cluster in cultural domains such as kinship terms beyond the nuclear family, agriculture, trade and social rank. They also tend to show phonological shapes that can be dated to particular stages of the donor language. Borrowing into the basic core of the lexicon is comparatively rare. The practical procedure, then, is cumulative. Linguists first establish which correspondences recur in inherited core vocabulary. They then test each similar word against those correspondences. Finally, they assign words that violate them, cluster in culturally transferable domains, or match a single donor stage to contact rather than to descent.
